summary.text: River-god of Elis, born to Oceanus and Tethys, who pursued the nymph Arethusa until she fled beneath the earth and rose as a spring on Ortygia at Syracuse — where Pausanias saw their waters said to mingle underground.

story.text: Hesiod names Alpheus among the eddying rivers Tethys bore to Ocean — set in one breath with Nile, Strymon, and Achelous in the first family of waters.

Ovid lets Arethusa tell the pursuit in Sicily. Once a Peloponnesian huntress, she bathed in Alpheus' stream until the river-god mingled his waters with hers and chased her in love; when she could run no more she prayed to Diana, the earth gaped, and she rose beneath Ortygia while Alpheus' voice still called after her through the chasm.

Pausanias knew the spring at Olympia where the Alpheius was said to mingle underground with Arethusa's Sicilian water — a marvel the god at Delphi confirmed when he sent Archias to found Syracuse at the place where Alpheius' mouth bubbles with Arethusa's springs.

Homer remembers Alpheus as father of Diocles of Pherae in the Odyssey's guest-friend passages — the river's mortal offspring on the Greek mainland, distinct from the Sicilian metamorphosis Ovid elaborates.
